rv.q: Metcalf supplies the gravitation that holds it all together, even as her immense centrifugal energy is, simultaneously, working to fling it all apart.

This is fearless acting, conveying the myriad painful human contradictions of a woman clinging to her formidable intellect like a life-raft while desperately trying to find a safe channel through the enveloping fog.

Operating within a honeycomb of overlapping wooden frames, Metcalf transforms from moment to moment and back again, from sublime competence to a helplessness that is hard to watch. But dare you to take your eyes off her.
Thanks to the superb performance of Laurie Metcalf as Juliana, the less we are sure of, the more we are engaged.

The play — so buffed and polished it now seems to squeak — is matched by a searing, brilliant performance by Laurie Metcalf, who is simply astonishing as she goes from snippy, bossy scientist to a broken, confused intruder wolfing down Chinese food on the floor.
The play is a vehicle for a valiant star, and Metcalf steers it with fearless confidence.
It is a breathtaking performance, but a wasted one.

Metcalf, White, and Mantello ensure that by the end of The Other Place , you'll know it intimately, and be grateful for even the most imposing nuances that prevent all escape while at the same time setting you free.
Bold, unflinching, and ingeniously constructed, this is a show not to be missed.
It's crackling theater, and it elevates the puzzle-like structure of White's plot into something with real emotional heft.
And as Juliana faces an uncertain future, audiences can be certain they're witnessing one of the season's greatest performances.
No one in New York can stage such a story better than the director here, Joe Mantello.

“The Other Place” satisfies and disturbs as it ties together the mystery involving Juliana’s daughter, and you’ll strain to wonder what goes through Metcalf’s mind, playing these particular moments opposite her own flesh-and-blood.
Metcalf, who earned an Obie Award in that earlier production, gives a performance as impressive for its elegance as it is for its fearlessness.
Metcalf, on the stage the entire play, holds our attention and our sympathy as she depicts a woman transformed...
The Other Place might lack poetry--or Wit--but its emotional moments are potent.
Like “The Great God Pan” earlier this season, “The Other Place” is yet another ambitious play that’s maddeningly unfinished.
The supporting cast is topnotch, including Daniel Stern as Juliana's beleaguered husband, Zoe Perry (Metcalf's real-life daughter)
With Metcalf's intense portrayal of a troubled doctor diluted in the much larger space, the work's contrivances and thinness are much more obvious.
With all due respect to Metcalf, who never leaves the stage and gives a brave and raw performance, "The Other Place" leaves much to be desired.
Quite an original and fascinating production.
The play’s superb structure and dialogue, as well as its other outstanding elements, make for a rich and compelling spectacle.

cn.t: Metcalf's powerhouse performance earns near-universal praise in this psychological drama, though some critics find White's script better suited to its Off-Broadway origins. Mostly positive reception overall.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
